title: On the performance of affine policies for two-stage adaptive optimization: a geometric perspective
contribution: Proves an a priori bound z_Aff <= λ(1+ρ/s)/(λ+ρ/s)·z_Adapt for affine policies in two-stage adjustable robust LPs with right-hand-side uncertainty, in terms of the uncertainty set's symmetry s, translation factor ρ and a new simplex dilation factor λ, and compares it with static-policy bounds and a posteriori instance bounds.
problem_entry: {RO+LO} Affine policies are tractable and do well empirically, but no general bound exists; the group's own bounds cover only static policies (1+ρ/s) or do not depend on U (O(√m) for affine); enter by adding a geometric constant tailored to affine policies (pp. 4-6).
key_idea: Simplex dilation factor λ(U), the smallest λ with a simplex S ∋ b0 and S ⊂ U ⊂ λ(S−b0)+b0; transport the affine policy that is optimal on S (Bertsimas-Goyal) to U by recentring and scaling; the bound is 1 at λ = 1 and tends to the static bound as λ grows (pp. 8, 10-12).
assumptions: Two stages, uncertainty only in the right-hand side, U convex compact in the nonnegative orthant, c, d >= 0 and nonnegative decisions (p. 4); λ given for balls (= m), p-norm balls and budget sets, with Lemma 5 proofs omitted (pp. 9-10); random inventory instances in the standard form (pp. 16-18).
proof_devices: Simplex dilation factor λ(U); λ = m for a ball (Lemma 4, pp. 9-10); λ <= m+2 for any convex body (Theorem 1 after Lagarias-Ziegler, p. 10)
Affine optimality on a simplex imported from Bertsimas-Goyal (Theorem 2, p. 10)
Lemma 6, α((b−b0)/λ + b0) >= b, derived from the symmetry-translation Lemma 3 (pp. 7, 10)
Policy transport: recentre the simplex-optimal affine policy at b0, scale the first stage by α and the slope by α/λ; cost chain z_Aff(U) <= α z_Adapt(S) <= α z_Adapt(U) (Theorem 3, pp. 11-12)
Bound tables for nine families of sets; for budget sets the affine bound is k²/(k²+m) of the static one (Tables 1-3, pp. 14-15)
Inventory model rewritten into the standard two-stage form by auxiliary variables (Lemma 7, pp. 16-18)
experiments: CPLEX 12.5; random inventory instances, a posteriori bound vs geometric affine bound vs static bound: Δ*(5,25) 2.78/3/5, Δ*(9,81) 3.21/5/9, DU*(3,9,9) 2.06/2.07/3; instance data posted online; some Table 4 cells merged in the extraction (pp. 16-19).
positioning: An a priori bound set against a posteriori approaches (Kuhn-Wiesemann-Georghiou; Hadjiyiannis-Goulart-Kuhn) and improving the group's own earlier bounds (Bertsimas-Goyal; Bertsimas-Goyal-Sun) for many standard sets (pp. 5-6, 14-15).
writing: The main bound is stated in the introduction before its constants are defined (p. 6); Lemma 5's proofs are omitted as not illuminating (p. 10); the evaluation is framed as showing the bound is informative (pp. 6, 18).
limits_future: Two stages and right-hand-side uncertainty only (p. 4); future: multistage and piecewise affine policies (p. 19); the a priori bound drifts away from the a posteriori one as k grows (Table 4, p. 19).

method_links.note: the class-keeping device (affine policies) is inherited, not designed; the paper prices it a priori through the geometry of U and prints the exact problem's O(log m) inapproximability

a price of a tractable policy class as a solution-independent bound, tabulated across standard sets and checked against instance bounds; no knob for a decision-maker and the widening gap at larger k is not discussed

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: own earlier result's limit as the entry
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Bertsimas-Goyal affine bounds do not depend on U and the Bertsimas-Goyal-Sun geometric bound covers static policies only; the paper adds the simplex dilation factor to cover affine policies

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a priori bound checked against instance-wise a posteriori bounds
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the geometric bound is set beside a posteriori bounds computed with the methods of Hadjiyiannis et al. and Kuhn et al. and beside the static bound on random inventory instances

transferable: To bound a restricted policy class, find a sub-object on which the class is exactly optimal (a simplex for affine policies), measure the real set's distance from it by one dilation constant, and transport the optimal policy by recentring and scaling (pp. 8, 10-12).
Tabulate the old bound, the new bound and their ratio for a catalogue of standard uncertainty sets so readers see where the gain is large (Tables 1-3, pp. 14-15).
Check an a priori worst-case bound against a posteriori bounds on random instances and publish the instance data (Table 4, p. 19).

quotes.text: While it has been observed empirically that these policies perform well in practice, to the best of our knowledge, there are no theoretical performance bounds for affine policies in general.
We find that the geometric a priori bound is quite close to the a posteriori bounds for random instances of the inventory control problem.

title: OR Forum—Tenure Analytics: Models for Predicting Research Impact
contribution: Predicts OR scholars' 9- and 16-year publication outcomes from their first five years with citation, coauthorship and dual-network centrality, and backtests the model as a tenure rule at the committees' capacity on 54 top-10 OR assistant professors, where it changes 30% of decisions and selects scholars with better projected outcomes.
problem_entry: {DA+ML+AP} Tenure decisions rest on subjective assessment; prediction studies use late-career data and none asks whether early-career predictions improve committees' decisions; enter with an OR bibliometric database and a backtest against actual tenure decisions (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Centrality (betweenness, closeness, clustering, PageRank) of papers and authors in citation, coauthorship and dual networks after five years feeds random forests; the tenure rule ranks scholars by average predicted rank over eight metrics and tenures as many as the committees did (pp. 4-5, 7-9).
assumptions: WOS OR papers 1975-2012 with name disambiguation (logistic model on WOS-SSRN matches, AUC 0.921; 19.9% lumping, 10.2% splitting on 166 checked scholars); 43,215 scholars for prediction (43,047 on p. 4), 70/30 split; a hand-built tenure set of 54 fixed before any comparison, labels checked by IRB-approved interviews; fixed tenure slots and projected 16-year outcomes from hierarchical linear models admitted as simplifications (pp. 3-7, 12-16).
proof_devices: n/a (empirical); evaluation devices: selection at matched capacity, the same number tenured as the committees (p. 9)
Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals for every comparison (pp. 8-10)
Modified MAPE dividing by max(y, 1) to handle zero outcomes (p. 8)
Balance check on secondary attributes (awards, teaching, editorships, gender, coauthors, subfields) (p. 12)
Log-log hierarchical linear models with random slopes and intercepts to project 16-year outcomes, R² 0.88-0.93 (pp. 15-16)
experiments: Centrality model more than halves MAPE vs a citation-only baseline on paper counts and predicts INFORMS fellows with AUC 0.97 vs 0.82 and 0.94; as a tenure rule it disagrees with committees on 16 of 54 and gains 1.3 A-journal papers, 38 citations and 0.8 h-index in projected 16-year outcomes; the four-metric model picks the same set; a 5-year-citation rule matches only on citations and h-index (pp. 8-12).
positioning: Moves from the h-index and late-career prediction literature (Hirsch; Acuna et al.; Penner et al.) to early-career decisions; network features motivated by information-flow and structural-holes work (Burt; Newman) (pp. 2-3).
writing: An OR Forum piece that calls for a 'Moneyball moment' in academia (p. 2); two numbered contributions (p. 3); a long section on limitations and implementation hurdles (pp. 12-13).
limits_future: Small sample; the tenure decision may itself change outcomes; fixed slots; OR and top-10 programmes only; deployment needs field-wide disambiguation, recalibration and guarding against gaming of centrality; committees might prefer the four-metric model, which tenures the same set (pp. 10, 12-13).

method_links.note: decisions, not predictions, are scored against the owner's current rule (tenure committees) at the same capacity on outcomes the owner values; a stronger naive rule (5-year citations) is also run; the evaluation's blind spot is printed and the use is framed as a decision aid; no field test

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the model selects as many scholars as the committees did from the same 54 candidates, and the realised (projected) outcomes of the two selected sets are compared

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: level the field and say which way it still tilts
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: matched tenure counts; the committees had forthcoming papers, teaching evaluations and letters the model lacked, a tilt the authors state is against the model

transferable: Backtest a predictor as a decision rule: give it the decision-maker's capacity and candidate pool and compare the realised outcomes of the two selected sets (mean and share of top performers) with bootstrap CIs (pp. 9-10).
Fix the evaluation cohort before running any comparison and say so (p. 5).
Add a balance table on secondary attributes so the new rule is shown not to shift them (p. 12).
Report whether the feature behind the prediction gains changes the decision at all (p. 10).
coauthors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Shachar Reichman, John Silberholz

quotes.text: Importantly, no studies to date have addressed whether early-career predictions of scholars’ future academic success can be used to improve the decisions made by tenure committees today.

Finally, the analysis treats the number of tenure slots across the programs studied as a fixed resource, an assumption made to simplify the comparison of the proposed model’s choices against those of tenure committees.

title: Robust fluid processing networks
contribution: Introduces a robust fluid model for multiclass processing networks with budgeted service-time and arrival-rate uncertainty that stays a separated continuous LP, derives a model-predictive robust fluid priority policy and a polynomial robust cμ-rule, and shows by simulation that it beats the nominal fluid policy in heavy traffic.
problem_entry: {SD+RO+LO} Optimal sequencing is an intractable stochastic DP, Brownian models are intractable beyond one dimension, and fluid models ignore variance; existing translations add uncertainty after the fact; enter by putting uncertainty inside the fluid control problem through robust optimization (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Budgeted interval uncertainty per server on service times and arrival rates; the robust counterpart is again an SCLP and arrival uncertainty drops out; re-solve at each epoch and prioritise by p*_i; robust cμ-rule by at most n LPs (pp. 5-9).
assumptions: Deterministic continuous fluid dynamics over [0, T] with linear constraints; budget-type uncertainty sets in continuous time; no distributional assumption for the policy; simulations with Poisson arrivals, exponential services, τ̃ = 0.25τ, c = e, and hyper-exponential variants with CoV 1.0-1.4 (pp. 2-5, 10-11).
proof_devices: Per-time LP duality on the inner maximization gives linear robust constraints (proof of Theorem 1, p. 6)
Worst-case arrival term independent of the control, so only nominal arrival rates matter (pp. 6-7)
Piecewise-constant single-server solution from a sequence of LPs, proved optimal by SCLP complementary slackness from Luo-Bertsimas (Theorem 2, pp. 8-9)
Deterministic case recovers the cμ-rule; Klimov's problem reduced to the same form by inverting A (p. 9)
Complexity note: SCLP NP-hard in general (contains min-cost dynamic flow) yet solvable at hundreds of variables (p. 7)
State-caching heuristic with tolerance ω to cut SCLP solves (pp. 9-10)
experiments: Simulations on criss-cross, six-class, reentrant feed-forward (m = 2-10) and reentrant (m = 2-7) networks vs exact DP where computable, optimized target-pursuing, best threshold, LBFS, FCFS, cμ and the nominal fluid policy: within 2.1% of the threshold policy and >12.7% better than the fluid policy in balanced heavy traffic; best Γ picked by simulation; table bodies missing from the extraction, hardware and run counts not stated in the text (pp. 10-12).
positioning: Between the Brownian (Harrison, Wein) and fluid (Dai, Avram-Bertsimas-Ricard, Meyn, Maglaras) traditions, using SCLP algorithms (Luo-Bertsimas, Pullan, Weiss) and RO (Ben-Tal et al., Bertsimas et al.) (pp. 1-2).
writing: Contributions labelled modelling power, insights and performance (p. 2); six numbered simulation conclusions (p. 12); one candid admission on stability (p. 13).
limits_future: Stability of the robust fluid policy not established and left open (p. 13); SCLP NP-hard in general (p. 7); Γ tuned by simulation (p. 10); scale claimed up to tens of classes and servers (p. 13).

method_links.note: a control problem owned by queueing and stochastic DP is written as an SCLP whose robust counterpart stays an SCLP; the dual reading shows arrival uncertainty is irrelevant; the boundary is printed (SCLP NP-hard in general, no stability proof)
Γ is the knob and its effect is plotted against CoV, but it is tuned per instance by simulation and carries no bound

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the robust single-server analysis gives an alternative proof of the cμ-rule's optimality, a robust cμ-rule, and the same for Klimov's problem

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Γ = 0 reduces the robust fluid model and policy to the classical fluid ones

transferable: Robustify the deterministic approximation (the fluid model) rather than the stochastic system, and prove the counterpart stays in the approximation's class so its solvers apply unchanged (Theorem 1, pp. 6-7).
Before modelling an uncertain parameter, check whether it drops out of the robust optimum (arrival rates, p. 7).
Test a heuristic policy against exact DP where it is computable and against the limit-regime policy in the regime that favours it (pp. 10-11).
Cache policies for visited states with a tolerance ω and plot solve counts against ω (Fig. 3, p. 11).

quotes.text: We show that the robust fluid model still remains within the class of SCLPs. Thus, it preserves the computational tractability of the classical fluid problem, and all solution techniques for SCLPs remain applicable.
Admittedly, we have not established stability of the class of robust fluid policies we introduced.

title: Optimizing over coherent risk measures and non-convexities: a robust mixed integer optimization approach
contribution: Minimizes coherent risk measures under a nonconvex norm equality by giving computable conditions under which the convex relaxation is exact and ℓ1/ℓ∞ MIO formulations otherwise, with leverage-constrained portfolio and Eν-SVM classification applications and a new Bregman-divergence coherent risk measure.
problem_entry: {RO+IO+ML+AP} Coherent risk minimization is RO over a set U; a norm equality fixes leverage in portfolios and excludes v = 0 in classification but is nonconvex, and practitioners were advised to leave such constraints out for lack of theory (pp. 1-3, 15).
key_idea: Either certify that the relaxation ‖v‖ <= c is exact (c <= τ with a strict value gap; for K = Rⁿ exactly when 0 ∉ U; one LP gives the CVaR threshold ν̂) or solve the ℓ1/ℓ∞ equality exactly as MIO with split variables and binaries (pp. 6-8, 13-14, 18-19).
assumptions: Finite scenario space with reference probabilities, bounded U, feasible c (Assumption 1); V convex or a cone; Nikkei 225 monthly (270 months) and weekly (1,178 weeks) returns in rolling windows; four UCI data sets (pp. 4-5, 7, 19-20, 25).
proof_devices: Convex-combination argument: an optimum of the relaxation strictly inside the norm ball can be improved toward the unconstrained optimum (Theorem 1, p. 6)
Sign of the optimal value decides exactness on cones (Lemma 1, p. 7)
Separating hyperplane links exactness to the position of 0 relative to U (Theorem 2, p. 8; weaker cone version Theorem 3, pp. 8-9)
LP duality of the inner maximization for scenario, CVaR and polyhedral or conic sets (pp. 10, 12-13)
Disjunctive MIO for ℓ1 and ℓ∞ equalities with v = v⁺ − v⁻ and bound c (eqs. (21)-(22), pp. 13-14)
Coherence restored by intersecting a set with conv(Z), giving a Bregman (squared Mahalanobis) measure (pp. 9-12)
experiments: Matlab R2011b + CPLEX 12 on a 2.3 GHz Core i7: rolling out-of-sample portfolios beat the model's own ablations (NormConst, NoNormConst) on test return, Sharpe ratio and turnover in all reported blocks, at higher return variance than NormConst; global ℓ1/ℓ∞ classifiers beat local ℓ2 Eν-SVM in most ν on four UCI sets but are slower when nonconvex; no MIO times or gaps tabulated (pp. 19-26).
positioning: Builds on Bertsimas-Brown and Natarajan et al. (risk measures as uncertainty sets) and generalizes norm-constrained portfolios (DeMiguel et al., Gotoh-Takeda, Brodie et al.) and CVaR-based SVMs (Takeda-Sugiyama, Gotoh et al.) (pp. 2-3).
writing: Three lettered claims (a)-(c) announce the computational results (p. 3); the theory section opens from a counter-recommendation in the practitioner literature (p. 3).
limits_future: ℓ2 norm stays hard (p. 13); MIO only at a proper problem size (p. 15); portfolio baselines are ablations plus a mean-standard deviation risk swap, no 1/N rule (pp. 20-24); Bregman advantage may not hold on other data; future: data-fitted uncertainty sets (p. 27).

method_links.note: a nonconvex constraint practitioners avoid is either certified away (exact convex relaxation under a computable condition) or written exactly as MIO; the boundary is printed (ℓ2 norm, problem size)
the exact global MIO duels the incumbent local-search Eν-SVM out of sample, but with no warm start, time limit, gap or certificate reported
reopens a constraint the literature advised leaving out, on the strength of MIO solvers, without a quantified why-now figure

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Rival method as a relaxation of the exact formulation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: ν-SVM is the convex relaxation of Eν-SVM and the norm-constrained portfolio model (24) relaxes (23); Theorem 2 states exactly when the relaxation is exact

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: hard-margin SVM, ν-SVM/Eν-SVM, mean-standard deviation and norm-constrained portfolio models appear as members of one coherent-risk family

transferable: Before branching on a nonconvex equality, solve the problem without it and compare the solution's norm with the target; a computable threshold tells when the convex relaxation is already exact (Theorem 1, p. 6; Remark 2, pp. 18-19).
Write ‖v‖₁ = c or ‖v‖∞ = c as MIO with split variables v⁺, v⁻, one binary per coordinate and a cover constraint for ∞ (pp. 13-14).
Intersect any convex uncertainty set with conv(Z) to make the induced risk measure coherent (pp. 9, 11-12).
Report how often the nonconvex case actually arises across rolling windows (nonconv.ratio, p. 22).

quotes.text: Though they recommended that such constraints be left out of analyses because there is no theory to support the required optimality conditions, we can obtain a global optimal solution for nonconvex portfolio optimization including leverage requirement by reformulating it as an MIO formulation.
As a future work, we want to consider a method for constructing a suitable uncertainty set U that fits to a dataset in each application.

title: Multistage robust mixed-integer optimization with adaptive partitions
contribution: Solves multistage adaptive MIO by finite adaptability whose partitions are Voronoi cells around the binding scenarios of the previous solution, iterated in nested and non-nested variants with nonanticipativity, with a scenario-based lower bound giving a gap, and beats prior AMIO methods on their own instances.
problem_entry: {RO+IO} Affine and polynomial rules cannot handle discrete recourse; the group's piecewise rules suffer fractionality and K-adaptability relies on big-M; solvable AMIO sizes lag far behind continuous adaptive optimization (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Read the active (minimum-slack) scenarios of the static cutting-plane solution, partition U by their Voronoi diagram, re-solve and repeat; a partition helps only if it separates the active scenarios (Theorem 1); nested and non-nested variants, affine rules mixed in, nonanticipativity enforced (pp. 8-17, 21).
assumptions: Linear constraints and objective in ξ, mixed-integer decisions, polyhedral U for polyhedral cells; instances taken from rivals' papers (capital budgeting, Hanasusanto et al.; multistage lot sizing, Bertsimas-Georghiou) plus a network extension; the improvement bound needs right-hand-side uncertainty and continuous problems (pp. 11, 41-50).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: no improvement unless the partition separates the active scenarios, by restricting to the active constraint set (pp. 9-10)
Voronoi cells as U plus N−1 linear cuts, no vertex enumeration needed (p. 11)
Scenario-based lower bound z_lower(A) <= z_full by mapping the fully adaptive policy onto the samples with nonanticipativity equalities, giving a gap-based stop rule (Proposition 3, pp. 34-35)
Non-monotone non-nested objectives shown by example (Proposition 4, p. 35); nested objectives monotone (p. 33; Proposition 5, p. 36)
Variable counts against the rival formulation: O(KN) binaries and O(2^K KN) continuous vs (1+2^(k−1))N binaries (p. 42)
experiments: Capital budgeting (20 instances): nested 77% improvement over static in 3.2 s at N = 10, non-nested 110% in 388 s at N = 40, matching Hanasusanto et al., whose method left almost all N = 20 unsolved in 2 h; gaps 18-34% after eight iterations; lot sizing (30 instances, T <= 10): average gap 15.5-24.7% to 9.3-16.2% in four iterations; network lot sizing with a 1,200 s limit and unsolved counts printed; solver, version and hardware not stated (pp. 41-51).
positioning: Between methods that optimize partitions (Bertsimas-Caramanis; Hanasusanto et al.) and a priori partitions (Vayanos et al.); the concurrent Postek-den Hertog method is acknowledged and contrasted (pp. 4-5, 21, 43).
writing: Closes with an analogy to branch and bound (restriction above, sampled relaxation below) (pp. 52-53); advises practitioners to try both variants (p. 33).
limits_future: Scenario lower bounds can be weak and need many scenarios, and AMIO lacks a cutting-plane-like advance (p. 52); nested does not dominate non-nested (p. 52); network instances with T = 6, N >= 3 unsolved within 1,200 s (Table 5, p. 51); future: local optimization of the partitions and warm starts across iterations (p. 53).

method_links.note: the partitioned problem is the nominal MIO with duplicated second-stage variables and no big-M or piecewise restructuring; the speed-up is attributed to preserving that structure; the boundary is printed (Table 5)
RO form of the protocol: every solution carries a gap against a lower bound on the fully adaptive optimum and rivals are dueled on their own instances, but no solver, version or machine is stated

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: own predecessor system's limit as the entry point
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the group's Bertsimas-Georghiou 2013 piecewise decision rules have significant trouble with fractionality as stages and pieces grow; the partitioning method starts there

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: binding scenarios bridge the restricted policy and the sampled lower bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: active scenarios of the current solution seed the Voronoi partitions, and the accumulated samples build the scenario-based lower bound that gives the gap; S138 in this batch does the same

transferable: Seed a Voronoi partition of the uncertainty set with the binding scenarios of the static robust solution; a partition that leaves all of them in one cell cannot help (Theorem 1, pp. 9-11).
Pair any restricted adaptive policy with a sampled relaxation that keeps nonanticipativity, and stop on the relative gap (Proposition 3, pp. 34-35).
Tabulate time, improvement and gap per iteration so readers can choose their own stopping point (Tables 1-2, p. 45).
Compare variable counts with the rival formulation, not only run times (p. 42).

quotes.text: While our method requires multiple solves and has more binary variables, we suggest the reason our approach is far more tractable is that it preserves the relatively simple problem structure, allowing the MIO solver to branch smarter and generate good solutions using heuristics.
We would draw an analogy again with integer optimization and the ability of cutting planes to significantly tighten the fractionality gap - AMIO has yet to see an equivalent development.

title: Duality in two-stage adaptive linear optimization: Faster computation and stronger bounds
contribution: Shows that dualizing a two-stage adaptive LO with fixed continuous recourse over the recourse and then over the uncertainty gives an equivalent two-stage adaptive LO whose affine policy maps to the primal one, solves an order of magnitude faster in two test problems, and strengthens the binding-scenario lower bound on affine-policy suboptimality.
problem_entry: {RO+LO} Affine policies are the tractable standard for two-stage adaptive LO and their suboptimality must be bounded per instance; the known one-step dualization over the recourse (Lemma 1) is taken one step further (pp. 2-4, 7).
key_idea: Dualize over recourse, then over the uncertain parameters: the result is again a two-stage adaptive LO with the same here-and-now decisions but swapped dimensions; affine policies are equivalent across the pair, so the cheaper side is solved and the other policy read off; binding scenarios of both policies strengthen the lower bound (pp. 4-8).
assumptions: Fixed recourse matrix, continuous recourse y >= 0, right-hand-side uncertainty in a polyhedron {ζ >= 0 : Dζ <= d} (extension to R(x) noted), integer first-stage decisions allowed; test problems: network lot sizing (N = 10-100, Γ = 20√N) and facility location (S = 10, C = 10-50) (pp. 3-4, 9, 11).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: dualize the recourse problem to a bilinear max over (ζ, w) (p. 4)
Second dualization over ζ for fixed w plus positive homogeneity to normalize w to a simplex (proof of Theorem 1, pp. 4-5)
Static case recovers the standard robust counterpart; linear policies optimal for a set with m extreme points (pp. 5-6)
Linear instead of affine dual policies without loss (Proposition 1, p. 6) and explicit variable maps between primal and dual affine counterparts (Theorem 2, pp. 6-7)
Counting affine constraints vs sign restrictions per formulation (Table 2, p. 7)
Algorithm 1: binding scenarios from both affine policies form one sampled lower-bound problem (pp. 7-8)
experiments: Gurobi 6.0.3, JuMP, i7-4770 3.40 GHz, 8 GB: dual an order of magnitude faster in lot sizing and the combined bound cuts the gap from 14.0-23.8% to 10.3-12.3%; adding constraints to U shrinks the speed-up until it disappears (counts equal at p = 400); facility location faster for larger instances, bounds only slightly better; random samples useless even at 10^5, cutting planes slower, bound weakest at Γ = 100% where static policies are optimal (pp. 7, 9-12).
positioning: Extends the known dualization used in Benders and column-generation work and the Hadjiyiannis et al. binding-scenario bound; notes that Kuhn et al.'s bound needs an a priori distribution (pp. 4, 7).
writing: Four numbered contributions (p. 3); a section titled as a question on why the dual is faster (pp. 9-10); a negative result reported as surprising (p. 12).
limits_future: Continuous fixed recourse and polyhedral U only (p. 3); bound gains problem-dependent (p. 10); the text's 'about 50 times' more affine constraints (p. 10) vs about 10 times in Table 5 as decoded (8,841 vs 882, consistent with Table 2's formulas); for C = 10 the dual is slower at three of six budgets (Table 6, p. 11).

method_links.note: dualizing twice keeps the problem in its class, dimensions are read off the dual, and the boundary is printed (fixed continuous recourse, polyhedral U)
the affine policy's suboptimality is certified by a sampled lower bound with solver, version and machine stated, and failures are printed; there is no out-of-sample duel with an incumbent

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: binding scenarios bridge the restricted policy and the sampled lower bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: binding scenarios of the primal and of the dual affine policy jointly form the sampled problem whose value bounds the fully adaptive optimum; random samples fail; also S087 in this batch

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: mechanism check by dialing the predicted cause
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the claimed cause of the speed-up (fewer affine constraints) is tested by adding constraints to U toward the point where both counts are equal (p = 400); the advantage shrinks and disappears

transferable: Dualize an adjustable robust LP twice, over the recourse and then over the uncertainty, to get an equivalent adjustable LP of different size, and apply existing methods to the smaller form (Theorem 1, p. 4; Table 1, p. 5).
Count affine constraints and sign restrictions separately for each formulation, since solvers treat them differently (Table 2, p. 7).
Test the explanation for a speed-up by varying the parameter it names toward the predicted crossover (Fig. 2, p. 10).
Build a sampled lower bound from scenarios that bind at the computed policies, not from random samples (p. 7; Algorithm 1, p. 8).
coauthors: Frans J. C. T. de Ruiter

quotes.text: The equivalent dualized formulation we derive is again a two-stage adaptive linear optimization model.
This is surprising, because for this case (box uncertainty) we know that affine (in fact, static) policies are provably optimal (Ben-Tal et al. 2009, Theorem 14.2.4).

title: On the power of randomization in network interdiction
contribution: Introduces randomized network interdiction, shows it equals the adaptive maximum-flow problem, derives complexity results, and proves tight ratios Γ+1, Γ+1 and Γ between deterministic and randomized interdiction values with approximations from one parametric LP.
problem_entry: {LO+IO+RO} Network interdiction (remove Γ arcs to minimize maximum flow) lets the flow player see the interdictor's pure strategy; enter by allowing the interdictor to randomize, a more realistic model for infrastructure protection (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: By minimax, randomized interdiction equals the adaptive maximum-flow problem in which the flow player commits first, so complexity transfers; a single LP that caps every arc's flow at θ and charges Γθ yields tight approximation ratios (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: Single-commodity s-t maximum flow with capacities; exactly Γ arcs removed; mixed strategies with finite support; arc-based and path-based flows coincide except in the randomized game (pp. 2-4).
proof_devices: Wald's minimax theorem plus concavity of the payoff in the flow (Theorem 1, pp. 3-4)
LP duality of the inner maximum flow for Γ = 1, giving one LP for the optimal mixed strategy (Theorem 5, p. 5)
Complexity imported from adaptive-flow results: strongly NP-hard in general, polynomial for fixed Γ, path-based NP-hard for Γ >= 2 (Theorems 3-4, p. 5)
Parametric LO with a per-arc cap θ (eq. (17), p. 5) and an exchange argument for Z_LO <= Z^Path_RNI (Lemma 1, pp. 5-6)
Perturbing θ* by ±ε counts arcs at the cap on two minimum cuts (Lemma 2, p. 6), giving the ratios (Lemmas 3-4, pp. 6-7)
Tightness via parallel-arc network families with ratio tending to the bound as K grows (pp. 7-8); path-based ratio by maximizing (29) over a and b (Theorem 7, p. 8)

This provides a more realistic model for various applications such as protecting critical infrastructures against terrorism or enemy’s attacks.

title: Certifiably optimal low rank factor analysis
contribution: Reformulates rank-constrained factor analysis with a PSD residual exactly as a smooth (and concave) semidefinite problem, computes high-quality solutions by conditional gradient, certifies them by a branch and bound with McCormick and Weyl bounds, and shows better estimates than standard R implementations.
problem_entry: {ML+CP+IO} Common FA estimators can return negative variances or an indefinite Σ − Φ, which breaks the explained-variance reading, and SDO-based methods scale only to p of about 20-30; enter by solving the full rank-constrained problem with certificates (pp. 1-7).
key_idea: Exact reformulations remove the rank constraint (eigenvalue problem in Φ, smooth problem over W with 0 ⪯ W ⪯ I and Tr W = p − r, concave minimization); conditional gradient gives upper bounds and a branch and bound with McCormick envelopes of W_ii φ_i and Weyl bounds gives certificates for q = 1 (pp. 8-17, 32).
assumptions: Any covariance or correlation matrix, no data assumptions; Schatten-q loss with q ∈ {1, 2} emphasized; synthetic classes A1, A2, B1-B3 with equal common and unique variance and five real data sets (pp. 1-3, 7, 25, 29, 37).
proof_devices: Exact reformulation as a nonsmooth eigenvalue problem in Φ (Proposition 1, p. 8) and as a smooth problem with convex compact constraints (Theorem 1, p. 9)
Partial minimization over Φ gives a concave function of W, enabling conditional gradient (Proposition 3, pp. 9-10)
Conditional-gradient stationarity and an O(1/K) rate (Theorems 2-3, pp. 12-13)
McCormick convex envelopes inside branch and bound, finite termination within additive TOL (Theorems 4-5, p. 16; Algorithm 3, p. 17)
Weyl's eigenvalue inequality for cheap root bounds and pruning (pp. 21, 32)
Special cases recover MRFA (q = 1), MTFA (q = 1, r = 0) and a PSD-constrained MINRES (q = 2) (p. 9)
experiments: Against psych/stats estimators (MINRES, WLS, PA, GLS, MLE, PC) and an own-ADMM MTFA, (CFAq) recovers Φ exactly and keeps Σ − Φ PSD where Category (B) methods do not; certificates in julia with MOSEK/SCS at additive TOL 0.1 and a 400,000 s cap on a shared cluster: most A1 instances certified at the root, A2 instances with p >= 20 and r* >= 3 hit the cap, p = 1,000-4,000 only root Weyl bounds with gaps 0.09-8.73 and no times (pp. 26-40).
positioning: Places (CFAq) among MTFA, MRFA, PC, MINRES, OLS/WLS/GLS, PA and MLE, grouped into SDO-based Category (A) and classical Category (B); compares its branch and bound with global-optimization software (BARON) and sets aside moment and copositive approaches (pp. 4-7, 24).
writing: First-paper claims in the abstract and contributions (pp. 1, 7) under the modern-optimization-lens brand (p. 7); a footnote explains why node counts accompany runtimes (p. 32).
limits_future: Certification cost grows with rank and p (p. 7); runtimes unreliable on the shared cluster and the implementation serial (p. 32); additive TOL 0.1 is large next to objectives of 0.06-1 (Table 2, p. 33); p. 30 credits Category (B) with the most explained variance while the Figure 3 caption credits (CFA1) (p. 32); future: other matrix-estimation problems (p. 43).

method_links.note: full protocol: a fast heuristic supplies the incumbent, an exact branch and bound certifies it with stated solvers, tolerance and cap, and the rival packages' standard estimators are the opponents; the heuristic stayed the incumbent in all but three instances; certificates are dropped at scale (A2 at the cap, p >= 1,000 root bounds only), while the contributions claim optimality proofs in minutes for some problems with p near 4000 and Table 11 shows no p = 4,000 root gap below 0.11 against the 0.1 tolerance used elsewhere

transferable: Replace a rank constraint by the variational form over {W : 0 ⪯ W ⪯ I, Tr W = p − r}, which makes the objective smooth or concave (Theorem 1, p. 9; Proposition 3, p. 10).
Compute two root bounds of different kinds (an envelope relaxation and an eigenvalue inequality) and keep the better per node (pp. 32-34).
When runtimes are noisy, report node counts beside times (p. 32, footnote 13).
Give every competitor a column for violation of the constraint the rivals ignore (λmin(Σ − Φ̂), Table 1, p. 28).

quotes.text: To our knowledge, this is the first paper that demonstrates how a previously intractable rank-constrained optimization problem can be solved to provable optimality by coupling developments in convex analysis and in discrete optimization.
It is particularly crucial to note that the optimal solutions for all problems we consider are found very quickly, and that vast majority of computational time is then spent on proving optimality.
